name: Alabama
origin: From the Alabama (Alibamu) people; often glossed from Choctaw as “thicket clearers.”

cities.name: Birmingham
cities.origin: Named for Birmingham, England, an ironworking center its founders hoped to rival.
cities.fact: Nicknamed the 'Magic City' for how fast it grew once local iron ore, coal, and limestone let it become the South's great steel town.

name: Alaska
origin: From Aleut/Unangan “Alaxsxaq” — roughly “the mainland.”

cities.name: Anchorage
cities.origin: Named for the ship anchorage on Cook Inlet used during construction of the Alaska Railroad.
cities.fact: Started as a tent camp for railroad workers and is now home to nearly 40% of the entire state's population.

name: Arizona
origin: Likely from O’odham “ali ṣonak” (small spring); a Basque origin is also proposed.

cities.name: Phoenix
cities.origin: Named by "Lord" Darrell Duppa for the mythical bird, since the town rose atop the ruins of the ancient Hohokam civilization's canals.
cities.fact: Those 1,000-year-old Hohokam canals were re-dug by the city's founders and are still the basis of part of the Valley's canal system today.

name: Arkansas
origin: A French rendering of a Sioux word for the Quapaw people.

cities.name: Little Rock
cities.origin: Named for "la petite roche," a small rock outcrop French explorer Bernard de la Harpe used as a river landmark in 1722.
cities.fact: That original little rock is still visible today, near the base of the Junction Bridge on the Arkansas River.

name: California
origin: From a mythical island in the 1510 Spanish romance “Las Sergas de Esplandián.”

sites.name: Golden Gate Bridge
sites.fact: When it opened it was the longest suspension-bridge span on Earth. Its “International Orange” color was chosen partly for visibility in San Francisco’s fog.

sites.name: Alcatraz Island
sites.fact: “The Rock” held Al Capone and George “Machine Gun” Kelly. No confirmed successful escape was ever proven; the 1962 escape remains officially unsolved.

sites.name: Yosemite National Park
sites.fact: Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant during the Civil War — the first time the U.S. set aside land specifically for preservation, seeding the national-park idea.

cities.name: Los Angeles
cities.origin: Founded by Spanish settlers as 'El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles' — 'the Town of Our Lady, Queen of the Angels.'
cities.fact: Its original 44 settlers were a small, ethnically mixed group of Spanish, Indigenous, and African ancestry recruited from Mexico.

name: Colorado
origin: Spanish for “colored/reddish,” after the silt-laden Colorado River.

cities.name: Denver
cities.origin: Named for Gen. James W. Denver, governor of Kansas Territory, by founders currying favor — he had actually already resigned before they arrived.
cities.fact: Its official elevation of 5,280 feet earns it the nickname 'the Mile High City'; a step on the State Capitol steps marks the exact spot.

name: Connecticut
origin: From Mohegan-Pequot “quinnitukqut” — “at the long tidal river.”

cities.name: Hartford
cities.origin: Named after Hertford, England, the hometown of an early settler.
cities.fact: Home to the oldest publicly funded park in America (Bushnell Park, 1854) and the insurance industry that gave it the nickname 'the Insurance Capital of the World.'

name: Delaware
origin: For Lord De La Warr (Thomas West), an early governor of Virginia.

cities.name: Wilmington
cities.origin: Named for Spencer Compton, Earl of Wilmington, when it received its borough charter.
cities.fact: Swedish colonists had already settled the site in 1638 as Fort Christina — one of the very first European settlements in the Delaware Valley.

name: Florida
origin: Spanish “Pascua Florida” (Feast of Flowers/Easter), named by Ponce de León in 1513.

sites.name: Castillo de San Marcos
sites.fact: In St. Augustine — the oldest masonry fort in the continental U.S. Its walls are coquina, a soft shell-stone that absorbed cannonballs instead of shattering.

sites.name: Kennedy Space Center
sites.fact: Launch site for every crewed U.S. Moon mission and the Space Shuttle. Launch Complex 39A sent Apollo 11 skyward on July 16, 1969.

sites.name: St. Augustine (Old Town)
sites.fact: The oldest continuously occupied European-established settlement in the continental U.S. — predating Jamestown by 42 years.

cities.name: Miami
cities.origin: From the Mayaimi people and Lake Mayaimi (now Lake Okeechobee), a name often glossed 'big water.'
cities.fact: Julia Tuttle, the only woman to found a major American city, convinced Henry Flagler to extend his railroad here after a hard 1894 freeze spared Miami's citrus.

name: Georgia
origin: Named for King George II of Great Britain.

cities.name: Atlanta
cities.origin: Began as 'Terminus,' the end of the line for the Western & Atlantic Railroad; the name Atlanta is a feminine form of 'Atlantic,' honoring that railroad.
cities.fact: It was burned during Sherman's 1864 March to the Sea and rebuilt so fast its later motto became 'Resurgens' — Latin for 'rising again.'

name: Hawaii
origin: Possibly from “Hawaiki,” the legendary Polynesian homeland.

cities.name: Honolulu
cities.origin: A Hawaiian name meaning 'sheltered bay' or 'calm port,' describing its harbor.
cities.fact: Became the capital of the Kingdom of Hawai'i under Kamehameha III in 1845, decades before statehood.

name: Idaho
origin: A coined word once claimed to be Shoshone; its true origin is disputed.

cities.name: Boise
cities.origin: From French-Canadian trappers' 'les bois' — 'the woods' — the trees along the river stood out amid otherwise dry, treeless plains.
cities.fact: Founded as a U.S. Army post to supply Oregon Trail travelers and nearby gold-rush miners.

name: Illinois
origin: French rendering of the name of the Illinois (Illini) confederation.

cities.name: Chicago
cities.origin: From the Miami-Illinois word 'shikaakwa,' referring to the wild garlic/onion that once grew along the riverbanks.
cities.fact: Rebuilt almost entirely after the Great Fire of 1871, it pioneered the modern skyscraper only a decade later.

name: Indiana
origin: Latin-style coinage meaning “Land of the Indians.”

cities.name: Indianapolis
cities.origin: A coined name meaning 'city of Indiana,' combining the state name with the Greek 'polis' (city).
cities.fact: It was deliberately platted from scratch as a new, centrally located state capital — there was no earlier town on the site.

name: Iowa
origin: From the Ioway (Iowa) people.

cities.name: Des Moines
cities.origin: Likely a French rendering of a Native word for the river (possibly 'Moingona'), later folk-etymologized as French for 'of the monks.'
cities.fact: Began as Fort Des Moines, a U.S. Army fort built at the junction of the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers.

name: Kansas
origin: From the Kansa (Kaw) people — “people of the south wind.”

cities.name: Wichita
cities.origin: Named for the Wichita people, who had villages in the area before American settlement.
cities.fact: Grew from a trading post on the Chisholm Trail into the self-proclaimed 'Air Capital of the World' for its aircraft manufacturing.

name: Kentucky
origin: From an Iroquoian word, often glossed “meadow land” or “land of tomorrow.”

cities.name: Louisville
cities.origin: Named for King Louis XVI of France, in gratitude for French support during the American Revolution.
cities.fact: Founded by George Rogers Clark on Corn Island in the Ohio River, right above the river's only natural falls.

name: Louisiana
origin: Named for King Louis XIV of France.

cities.name: New Orleans
cities.origin: Named for Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who was regent of France when the city was founded.
cities.fact: Built on a crescent bend of the Mississippi, which is why its oldest neighborhoods are still called 'the Crescent City.'

name: Maine
origin: Likely the nautical “mainland,” or the French province of Maine.

cities.name: Portland
cities.origin: Renamed from 'Falmouth Neck' after the Isle of Portland on the English coast.
cities.fact: Burned to the ground four times — including by the British in 1775 and the Great Fire of 1866 — and rebuilt each time.

name: Maryland
origin: For Queen Henrietta Maria, wife of King Charles I.

cities.name: Baltimore
cities.origin: Named for the Barons Baltimore, the Calvert family who held Maryland's founding proprietorship.
cities.fact: Its Fort McHenry survived a British bombardment in 1814 that inspired Francis Scott Key to write 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'

name: Massachusetts
origin: From the Massachusett people — “at/near the great hill.”

sites.name: Faneuil Hall
sites.fact: Boston’s “Cradle of Liberty” — the meeting hall where colonists debated resistance to British taxes in the years before the Revolution.

sites.name: Plymouth Rock
sites.fact: The traditional landing spot of the Mayflower Pilgrims. The rock now sits under a granite portico at the water’s edge.

sites.name: USS Constitution
sites.fact: “Old Ironsides” — the world’s oldest commissioned warship still afloat. British shot seemed to bounce off her oak hull in the War of 1812.

cities.name: Boston
cities.origin: Named after Boston, Lincolnshire, England, hometown of many Puritan settlers.
cities.fact: Founded by the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony as their new 'city upon a hill.'

name: Michigan
origin: From Ojibwe “mishigami” — “large water” (the Great Lakes).

cities.name: Detroit
cities.origin: French for 'strait,' after the narrow Detroit River connecting Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie, where Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac built his fort.
cities.fact: Became 'Motor City' in the early 1900s once Ford, Olds, and the Dodge brothers all built car factories along that same river.

name: Minnesota
origin: From Dakota “mni sota” — “cloudy” or “sky-tinted” water.

cities.name: Minneapolis
cities.origin: Blends Dakota 'mni' (water) with the Greek 'polis' (city) — a nod to nearby Saint Anthony Falls.
cities.fact: Its milling district around those falls once made it the flour-milling capital of the world, powering brands like Pillsbury and General Mills.

name: Mississippi
origin: From Ojibwe “misi-ziibi” — “great river.”

cities.name: Jackson
cities.origin: Named for Andrew Jackson, hero of the Battle of New Orleans, before he became president.
cities.fact: Chosen as capital largely for its central location and site on the Pearl River, replacing Natchez.

name: Missouri
origin: From the Missouria people — “people of the big canoes.”

cities.name: Kansas City
cities.origin: Named, like the state of Kansas, for the Kansa (Kaw) people, whose name is often glossed 'people of the south wind.'
cities.fact: Sits at the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas Rivers and is famous for more fountains than any city besides Rome.

name: Montana
origin: From Spanish/Latin “montaña” — “mountain.”

cities.name: Billings
cities.origin: Named for Frederick H. Billings, president of the Northern Pacific Railroad, whose line reached the site that year.
cities.fact: Grew so fast after the railroad arrived that it earned the nickname 'the Magic City.'

name: Nebraska
origin: From Otoe/Omaha “ñí brásge” — “flat water” (the Platte River).

cities.name: Omaha
cities.origin: Named for the Omaha people, whose own name is often translated 'those going against the current' or 'upstream people.'
cities.fact: Its Union Pacific headquarters made it the eastern starting point of the First Transcontinental Railroad in 1863.

name: Nevada
origin: Spanish “nevada” — “snow-covered,” from the Sierra Nevada.

cities.name: Las Vegas
cities.origin: Spanish for 'the meadows,' after natural artesian springs that once made the site a green oasis in the desert.
cities.fact: Its founding date marks a railroad land auction; Hoover Dam construction in the 1930s is what later brought its population boom.

name: New Hampshire
origin: Named for the English county of Hampshire.

cities.name: Manchester
cities.origin: Renamed from Derryfield after Manchester, England, in hopes of rivaling that city's textile-mill industry.
cities.fact: The Amoskeag Manufacturing Company built along the Merrimack River here became, for a time, the largest cotton-textile plant on Earth.

name: New Jersey
origin: Named for the Channel Island of Jersey.

cities.name: Newark
cities.origin: Likely named for Newark-on-Trent, England, the hometown of a founding Puritan minister.
cities.fact: Founded by Connecticut Puritans led by Robert Treat seeking a stricter religious community than Connecticut allowed.

name: New Mexico
origin: Spanish “Nuevo México,” used long before the modern country of Mexico existed.

cities.name: Albuquerque
cities.origin: Named for the Duke of Alburquerque, viceroy of New Spain, though the first 'r' later dropped from spelling.
cities.fact: Founded as a Spanish colonial villa along the Rio Grande and the Camino Real trade route to Mexico City.

name: New York
origin: For the Duke of York (later King James II), after the English took New Amsterdam.

sites.name: Statue of Liberty
sites.fact: A gift from France designed by Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi. Its internal iron skeleton was engineered by Gustave Eiffel, who later built his tower in Paris.

sites.name: Ellis Island
sites.fact: The nation’s busiest immigration station until 1954 — roughly 12 million people passed through its Great Hall on their way into America.

sites.name: 9/11 Memorial & One WTC
sites.fact: Twin reflecting pools sit in the footprints of the original towers. One World Trade Center rises to 1,776 feet — a nod to 1776.

sites.name: Niagara Falls State Park
sites.fact: The oldest state park in the United States, laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted — the landscape architect behind Central Park.

cities.name: New York City
cities.origin: Founded by the Dutch as New Amsterdam; renamed New York in 1664 for the Duke of York after the English seized it.
cities.fact: Its Dutch roots still show in names like Brooklyn (Breukelen), Harlem (Haarlem), and Wall Street (built along a defensive wall).

name: North Carolina
origin: For King Charles I (Latin “Carolus”).

cities.name: Charlotte
cities.origin: Named for Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, wife of Britain's King George III.
cities.fact: Ironically became a hotbed of Revolutionary sentiment so fierce that Lord Cornwallis called it 'a hornet's nest of rebellion.'

name: North Dakota
origin: From the Dakota (Sioux) people — “friend/ally.”

cities.name: Fargo
cities.origin: Named for William Fargo, co-founder of Wells, Fargo & Co. and a director of the Northern Pacific Railroad.
cities.fact: Began as a rough railhead camp nicknamed 'Fargo in the Timber' before the Northern Pacific bridged the Red River there.

name: Ohio
origin: From Seneca “ohi:yo’” — “great river.”

cities.name: Columbus
cities.origin: Named for Christopher Columbus when the Ohio legislature chose the site as a brand-new, centrally located capital.
cities.fact: Like Indianapolis, it was platted on forest land with no prior town — built specifically to be the capital.

name: Oklahoma
origin: From Choctaw “okla humma” — “red people.”

cities.name: Oklahoma City
cities.origin: Shares the state's name, from Choctaw 'okla humma' — 'red people.'
cities.fact: Went from empty prairie to a tent city of roughly 10,000 people in a single afternoon during the Land Run of April 22, 1889.

name: Oregon
origin: Origin genuinely uncertain; several competing theories exist.

cities.name: Portland
cities.origin: Chosen by a coin flip between founders Asa Lovejoy (who wanted 'Boston') and Francis Pettygrove (who wanted 'Portland,' after his Maine hometown).
cities.fact: That 1845 coin — the 'Portland Penny' — still survives and is on display at the Oregon Historical Society.

name: Pennsylvania
origin: “Penn’s Woods” — honoring Admiral William Penn, father of founder William Penn.

sites.name: Independence Hall
sites.fact: In Philadelphia — both the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the U.S. Constitution (1787) were debated and adopted inside this red-brick building.

sites.name: Liberty Bell
sites.fact: Famous for its jagged crack. Its inscription — “proclaim liberty throughout all the land” — made it an icon for abolitionists in the 1800s.

sites.name: Gettysburg Battlefield
sites.fact: Site of the Civil War’s bloodiest battle and, months later, Lincoln’s 272-word Gettysburg Address.

cities.name: Philadelphia
cities.origin: Coined by William Penn from Greek 'philos' (love) + 'adelphos' (brother) — 'the City of Brotherly Love.'
cities.fact: Penn personally laid out its original grid plan, one of the first planned cities in the American colonies.

name: Rhode Island
origin: Possibly for Aquidneck’s likeness to Rhodes, or Dutch “Roodt Eylandt” (red island).

cities.name: Providence
cities.origin: Named by founder Roger Williams in gratitude for what he called 'God's merciful Providence' after his banishment from Massachusetts.
cities.fact: Williams founded it explicitly on principles of religious liberty, a radical idea for New England in the 1630s.

name: South Carolina
origin: For King Charles I (Latin “Carolus”).

cities.name: Charleston
cities.origin: Originally 'Charles Town,' named for England's King Charles II.
cities.fact: Its harbor forts, including Fort Sumter, saw the opening shots of the Civil War in April 1861.

name: South Dakota
origin: From the Dakota (Sioux) people — “friend/ally.”

cities.name: Sioux Falls
cities.origin: Named for the waterfalls on the Big Sioux River and the Sioux (Dakota/Lakota) people.
cities.fact: Those falls, now the centerpiece of Falls Park, once powered the city's early quartzite-milling industry.

name: Tennessee
origin: From the Cherokee town name “Tanasi.”

cities.name: Nashville
cities.origin: Named for Francis Nash, a Revolutionary War general killed in the 1777 Battle of Germantown.
cities.fact: Began as Fort Nashborough, a river-bluff stockade built by James Robertson and John Donelson's parties.

name: Texas
origin: From Caddo “táysha” — “friends/allies.”

sites.name: The Alamo
sites.fact: A former Spanish mission in San Antonio. Its 1836 siege — and the cry “Remember the Alamo!” — became the rallying point of the Texas Revolution.

sites.name: San Jacinto Monument
sites.fact: Marks where Texas won its independence in an 18-minute battle. At 567 feet, the column is topped by a Lone Star and stands taller than the Washington Monument.

cities.name: Houston
cities.origin: Named for Sam Houston, hero of the Battle of San Jacinto and first president of the Republic of Texas.
cities.fact: Founded by land-speculating Allen brothers just weeks after San Jacinto, betting the new republic would need a capital-sized city.

name: Utah
origin: From the Ute people.

cities.name: Salt Lake City
cities.origin: Named for the adjacent Great Salt Lake.
cities.fact: Founded by Brigham Young's Mormon pioneers within days of reaching the valley, fleeing religious persecution in Illinois.

name: Vermont
origin: From French “vert mont” — “green mountain.”

cities.name: Burlington
cities.origin: Possibly honors the Burling family, prominent New York investors in the original Vermont land grants.
cities.fact: Its lakefront on Lake Champlain made it Vermont's busiest 19th-century port for lumber and grain.

name: Virginia
origin: For Elizabeth I, England’s “Virgin Queen.”

cities.name: Richmond
cities.origin: Named by founder William Byrd II after Richmond upon Thames, England, whose river view reminded him of the James River here.
cities.fact: Served as the capital of the Confederacy from 1861 until it fell to Union troops in April 1865.

name: Washington
origin: For George Washington — the only U.S. state named after a president.

cities.name: Seattle
cities.origin: Named for Chief Si'ahl (anglicized 'Seattle') of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples.
cities.fact: Rebuilt in brick and stone after the Great Seattle Fire of 1889 destroyed nearly its entire downtown core.

name: West Virginia
origin: Split from Virginia during the Civil War; keeps the Virginia name.

cities.name: Charleston
cities.origin: Named for Charles Clendenin, father of city founder George Clendenin.
cities.fact: Became the capital of the new state of West Virginia in 1863, after the western counties split from Confederate Virginia.

name: Wisconsin
origin: A French rendering of a Miami/Ojibwe river name; exact meaning uncertain.

cities.name: Milwaukee
cities.origin: From an Algonquian word often glossed 'good land' or 'gathering place by the water.'
cities.fact: Formed by merging three rival townships and went on to become a beer-brewing capital thanks to its many German immigrant settlers.

name: Wyoming
origin: From a Delaware (Lenape) word for “large prairie place,” via Pennsylvania’s Wyoming Valley.

cities.name: Cheyenne
cities.origin: Named for the Cheyenne Nation.
cities.fact: Sprang up almost overnight as a Union Pacific Railroad camp, earning the nickname 'Magic City of the Plains.'

name: Washington, D.C.
origin: “Columbia” honors Christopher Columbus; the District was established by the Residence Act of 1790.

sites.name: Lincoln Memorial
sites.fact: Its 19-foot marble Lincoln faces the Mall. On its steps in 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the “I Have a Dream” speech.

sites.name: Washington Monument
sites.fact: A 555-foot marble obelisk. A funding gap mid-build left a visible color change in the stone about a third of the way up.

sites.name: U.S. Capitol
sites.fact: Home of Congress. Its cast-iron dome was completed during the Civil War — Lincoln insisted work continue as a sign the Union would endure.

sites.name: The White House
sites.fact: Every president except George Washington has lived here. British troops burned it in 1814; it was rebuilt and reoccupied by 1817.

cities.name: Georgetown
cities.origin: Chartered by the Maryland colonial legislature and named for King George II.
cities.fact: Already a busy tobacco port decades before the federal district existed — it was folded into Washington in 1871.
